title: Strict Mode & tsconfig
subtitle: strict flag, strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, and essential tsconfig options
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: TypeScript's default settings are lenient — to ease migration from JavaScript. But lenient defaults (any inference, nullable everywhere) defeat the purpose of TypeScript for new projects.
whyItExists.solution: strict: true enables all strict mode checks in one line. strictNullChecks prevents null/undefined from sneaking into typed variables. noImplicitAny prevents TypeScript from silently using any when it can't infer a type. These flags catch far more bugs.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Always. Start every new TypeScript project with strict: true in tsconfig.json. You'll thank yourself later.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When migrating a large existing JavaScript codebase — you might turn on strict flags incrementally. But for new code, strict: true from day one.

explainModes.beginner: TypeScript has a setting called strict mode that turns on all the strictest checks. Without it, TypeScript misses some bugs. With it, TypeScript catches many more errors before your code runs. Think of it as 'extra careful mode'.
explainModes.simple: tsconfig.json: { 'compilerOptions': { 'strict': true } } — enables all strict checks. strict: true is a shorthand for: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis. noUncheckedIndexedAccess: arr[i] type is T | undefined, not T. exactOptionalPropertyTypes: optional prop can't be explicitly set to undefined.
explainModes.standard: strictNullChecks is the most impactful: without it, null is assignable to string (like Java). With it, string | null is required. noImplicitAny: TypeScript must be able to infer the type, or you must annotate it. Prevents implicit any in callbacks and parameters. target and lib: target controls emitted JS version. lib controls which browser/runtime APIs are available in types. Useful: lib: ['ES2022', 'DOM'] for browser code, lib: ['ES2022'] for Node.js.
explainModes.technical: strict: true flags included: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes (prevents method bivariance), strictBindCallApply (types .call/.bind/.apply correctly), strictPropertyInitialization (class properties must be initialized in constructor). Additional recommended flags: noUncheckedIndexedAccess (arrays and index signatures return T | undefined), exactOptionalPropertyTypes (option?: T means T, not T | undefined when assigning), noImplicitReturns (all code paths in function must return), noFallthroughCasesInSwitch.
explainModes.deepDive: tsconfig.json extends: most monorepos have a base tsconfig that projects inherit and override. Composite projects (composite: true): enables TypeScript project references for large codebases — each subproject has its own tsconfig, and tsc only recompiles what changed. incremental: true caches the last compilation to speed up rebuilds (.tsbuildinfo file). skipLibCheck: true skips type checking of .d.ts files — useful when third-party types have bugs, but hides your own declaration errors. isolatedModules: true — required by esbuild/swc because they compile files in parallel without a full type pass.

questions.question: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true`, what is the type of `arr[0]` when `arr: string[]`?
questions.explanation: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, accessing an array by index returns T | undefined — because the index might be out of bounds. Without this flag, TypeScript assumes arr[i] always returns T (not undefined), which can lead to runtime errors when the index is invalid. This flag makes TypeScript much safer for array operations.

faq.q: My existing project has many strict mode errors. How do I enable strict incrementally?
faq.a: Instead of strict: true, enable individual flags one at a time: start with noImplicitAny (highest value), then strictNullChecks (most impactful), then the others. Fix errors for each flag before enabling the next. Alternatively, use // @ts-check in JS files or ts-migrate tool to do the migration semi-automatically.

examples: All React projects created with create-react-app or Vite have strict: true by default
Library projects: declaration: true, declarationMap: true, sourceMap: true
